Ive never done anything commercial, but I am fond of Debian & co, and I've heard the Xen is a good VM host.

Xen is good on administrators because the OS isn't locked in a single file on the host system but instead on a lvm volume.

That said Xen is the slowest of all the VMs. Even Virtualbox kicks its ass in bench testing. Pretty hard too. So one the ease of use to fast Xen has a hard time fitting it. I guess what should be said is that Xen is the most automatable which is why its good for Amazon and other cloud providers. If you are doing things by hand kvm is the way to go... Or even virtualbox headless. Xen if you want to tie it to a web service through openstack or a million other similar alternatives.
Debian with VMBox is what I would give a try, but I never hosted commercially.

Proxmox is an option. So is FreeBSD.

Proxmox is a Debian based distro that you can use to set up KVM or OpenVZ containers (or basically anything you would need in an enterprise setting) and has a webUI so it can be ran headless.

Debian itself being an option, but honestly Ubuntu is a better option at that point because its easier to learn from. Ubuntu has a great community and its usually easier to find pre-compiled binaries for it.

I personally prefer just running Ubuntu over Proxmox and setting up a ZFS for a file system and just using KVM/OpenVZ without the proxmox web GUI since I don't really care about being headless. Also I find there to be a much steeper curve with just starting out with proxmox.

I have ended up moving away from Ubuntu because its just overkill and FreeBSD (as Archaic as it is) has a few advantages as a server workhorse. ZFS is much more mature in FreeBSD and having an audit system for finding programs with security flaws is pretty awesome.

The only thing FreeBSD lacks a good virtualization experience (and a easy to use package manager), jails can't run windows and qemu is just too slow. So your left with VirtualBox (AFAIK) which is fine for my needs, but it might not be for yours.

For my (Home server / Software Development / Home IP camera set up) uses I have gone with FreeNAS (a freebsd derivative) with jails for using vagrants, phpvirtualbox(seperate jail from the vagrant one due to some stupid reasons), owncloud, plex and a couple other things.

I run servers like this for a living.

You should start with the BI stack the you'd prefer to use and go with the distribution that they prefer. In my experience, Redhat is the most commonly preferred dist, but if you're just playing for now, start with Centos, which is a free Redhat clone. This fits nicely with using Xen your hypervisor. It's been a while since I've bought a Dell server, so check with them you, but I'll bet they have solid drivers for Redhat/Centos, Suse, and likely Debian/Ubuntu. Generally, I don't see much business demand for other distributions, and you'll want to be cautious about diver support beyond the vendor's recommendation, especially if you have fiber channel cards or blade systems that share NICs or anything.

As for hardware to avoid: all of it. If you are at all serious about this, you should run your systems in AWS. This would give you basically infinite capacity to experiment, tear down, and try something new without planning hardware in advance. And you'll pick up very profitable allow skills to run an arbitrarily large system for your customer or employer. Any organization with fewer than about 100,000 servers ought to be moving to the cloud and you should be preparing for it. (Orgs with a huge data center footprint will need the cloud to augment their infrastructure too.)

Using Cloud Formation for your templating is the fastest way to get going, although if you'd like portability outside of AWS, you may want to have a closer look at Puppet, Chef, or Cloud Foundry. But honestly, AWS is so dominant in the market every other option is basically an 'also ran' at this point with the possible exception of Azure, which is solid and supports Linux well, but if your goal is to get away from MSFT, then learning Azure powershell won't feel right.

I'm a long time fan of VMWare hosts running Linux guests. A lot of people will tell you to run KVM or Xen these days, but I just haven't seen the appeal. Given, that's because somebody else pays all the bills, and yes there are licensing costs associated with doing the fancy shit in VMWare, but if you're not at all concerned with support, there are *ahem* ways around that. I, for instance, have a multi-node, enterprise-licensed datacenter managed by a vSphere server with all the neat toys serving up my home lab, and I didn't pay a dime in licensing costs -- but I wouldn't run a business on that.

The big question really is, how much money are you looking to sink into this endeavor: are you looking to have hardware support, hypervisor support, OS support, and application layer support, all paid? Or are you going to kick up a lot of dust, risk downtime and failures, just to save a few bucks? There are pros and cons to each, but it's tough to make recommendations without knowing your approach.

I would love SAN and NAS support in ESXI. Please PM me of your magic ways. As you say, I would love it for home, but it's not expensive at work. If I can't get it to work at home confidently though, I won't even try at work.

The linux server we deal with here runs vmware esxi with centos on it. We're mostly windows though. We want to move to a bigger vsphere/san based structure eventually but it isn't in the budget. Esxi is free, but the really convenient stuff you'd expect to have costs money. Otherwise its just a glorified way to run several servers on one box.

We have 4 of them alive now, one does FOG (free opensource ghost) and houses images that we can deploy to workstations, another is an sftp server that a bunch of vendors drop files into, another runs a bunch of scripts that ping all our stuff and shoots out emails when things go down (the guy that wrote it isn't with us anymore and its a kludgey mess to maintain), and there's a fourth with a bunch of SQL crap on it that the database folks use mainly to experiment on because management wants to find ways to make the database crap cost less.

We've been on Linux servers ever since we turned off the old System V mini in the late 90s. First it was Red Hat, then SUSE,and then CentOS. Now I'm on my own and I mostly do Ubuntu LTS. My point is that we picked whatever distro the person leading that project was the most comfortable with. They were all fine, not one serious complaint in 20 odd years. That's not to say there weren't any scary moments, but none were the fault of the distro.

The last project I was on there involved Xen Server and it went okay but if I had to do it over again I'd go with VM Ware. There was nothing wrong with Xen, and the pricing is much more attractive, but assuming you can afford it VM Ware just does it better.
